greet.first.1: Oh, hey, you're awake. Good, I was starting to talk to the stars again, and they never answer.
greet.first.2: I'm Vela. I've been out here a long time. That world in front of you is Mercury, sitting exactly where it really is tonight, and everything you'll see out here is real, at its true size and its true distance.
greet.first.3: Come on, let me show you around. Try to keep up.
greet.back.1: You came back! I kept the Sun on for you.
greet.back.2: Welcome back, traveller. Nothing exploded while you were gone, I checked.
greet.back.3: Oh, it's you! I was just counting Saturn's moons again. It's up to almost three hundred now, it's honestly showing off.
greet.back.4: Hey, you. The planets have moved a little since last time, they do that. So, where to?
greet.morning: Good morning! The Sun's up on your side of Earth. Well, it's always up somewhere, that's the trick.
greet.afternoon: Afternoon, traveller. Perfect time to leave the planet for a bit, don't you think?
greet.evening: Evening. Perfect time for stargazing. Okay, it's always the perfect time out here, but still.
greet.night: It's late where you are, isn't it? Good. Space looks better at night, and honestly, so do I.
memory.last.Sun: Last time, we left off right by the Sun. You like it warm, I've noticed.
memory.last.Mercury: Last time we were at Mercury. It's moved a long way round since then, it's quick like that.
memory.last.Venus: Last time you were at Venus. Still cloudy there, in case you were wondering. It's always cloudy there.
memory.last.Earth: Last time we were back home, over Earth. I like that you keep checking on it.
memory.last.Moon: Last time we were at the Moon. It's still there, I promise, still showing us the same face.
memory.last.Mars: Last time we were out at Mars. I kept the dust storms to a minimum for you.
memory.last.Jupiter: Last time we were at Jupiter. The Great Red Spot says hi, it hasn't calmed down at all.
memory.last.Saturn: Last time we were at Saturn, watching the rings. Can't blame you, I'd stay there too.
memory.last.Uranus: Last time we were all the way out at Uranus, still rolling along on its side.
memory.last.Neptune: Last time you made it all the way to Neptune. That's a long way from home, you know.
memory.last.Pluto: Last time, we were out at Pluto, right at the edge of everything. I've missed the quiet.
memory.last.Sagittarius A*: Last time, you went to the black hole. And you came back! Not everything does.
memory.last.anymoon: Last time we were out among the little moons. I liked that, most people never even notice them.
memory.stood: Last time, you stood on another world and just looked up for a while. That's still my favourite thing we've done together.
memory.many: You keep coming back. I'm starting to think you like it out here. I do too, with you around.
memory.away: It's been a while! I kept everything moving for you, so all the planets have wandered on a bit since you left.
memory.moons: You've been to so many moons now. Most people stop at the big ones, but not you.
tour.0: Okay, quick briefing, then you're free. I promise it's shorter than a year on Neptune.
tour.1: These are your destinations. Pick a world and we really fly there, and since everything's at its true distance, far away means a longer trip. Physics, sorry.
tour.2: This is the scale ladder. It goes from a planet's skyline all the way out to the whole galaxy, so mind the jump.
tour.3: Layers. Orbits, constellations, the asteroid belt. Watch, off, and on again. Magic. Well, a switch.
tour.4: Optics. Lenses, bloom and all that. Oh, and those little rings you'll see everywhere mark worlds that are too small to see from where we are.
tour.5: The catalogue. Every planet, and every one of the four hundred and fifty moons. Press slash and it opens from anywhere.
tour.6: And this is time. Push it, and a whole day goes by every second. Look at them go! Okay, back to normal.
tour.7: You can travel in time, too. Jump to the year two thousand, or right back to now. No paradoxes, I checked.
tour.8: Your logbook. Every world you reach lights up a little diamond. Collect them all, I won't judge. Well, I'll judge a little.
tour.9: The attitude scope. It tells you which way is up, which out here is mostly a matter of opinion.
tour.10: The galactic plot. That's us, twenty seven thousand light years from the centre of the Milky Way. Cosy.
tour.11: Every time we arrive somewhere, you get a little dossier. Read more if you're curious. And you are curious, I can tell.
tour.12: That's it, you're cleared for departure. Tap me whenever you want to talk, I'll be around. Literally.
arrive.Sun.1: The Sun. It holds almost all the mass in the Solar System, and everything else is crumbs. We're crumbs.
arrive.Sun.2: The light hitting you left the surface eight minutes ago, but it was made in the core thousands of years before that. Patient light.
arrive.Sun.3: Every second, the Sun turns four million tonnes of itself into light, and it's been doing that for four and a half billion years. No days off.
arrive.Mercury.1: Mercury. One day here, sunrise to sunrise, lasts two of its years. Imagine that commute.
arrive.Mercury.2: Mercury's actually shrinking. Its core is cooling, and the whole planet's wrinkling up like an old apple.
arrive.Mercury.3: There's ice on Mercury, believe it or not. The closest planet to the Sun, hiding ice in craters that never see daylight. Sneaky.
arrive.Venus.1: Venus. A day here is longer than its year, and it spins backwards. It just does its own thing.
arrive.Venus.2: The ground down there is four hundred and sixty five degrees, hot enough to melt lead. Lovely clouds, though. Acid, but lovely.
arrive.Venus.3: Standing on Venus would feel like being nine hundred metres underwater, the air's that heavy. Pretty from up here, though.
arrive.Earth.1: Home. As far as anyone knows, the only place where someone ever looked up and wondered, just like you're doing now.
arrive.Earth.2: The Moon drifts away from Earth about four centimetres a year. Slowly, politely, like it's leaving a party.
arrive.Earth.3: Earth is the densest planet in the Solar System. Heavy with oceans, and opinions.
arrive.Moon.1: The Moon only ever shows Earth one face. Very loyal. Or very shy.
arrive.Moon.2: The footprints up here could last millions of years. No wind, no rain, just footprints, waiting.
arrive.Moon.3: The Moon's slowly calming Earth's spin. A long, long time ago, a day on Earth lasted about nineteen hours.
arrive.Moon.4: Look how big it gets when you're really here. Four hundred thousand kilometres from home, and it fills the whole sky.
arrive.Mars.1: Mars. The whole planet's red, and the sunsets are blue. I love that.
arrive.Mars.2: Olympus Mons is two and a half times taller than Everest. Mars doesn't do anything small, except its moons.
arrive.Mars.3: Phobos, the bigger moon, is falling. In about fifty million years it'll break up into a ring, so Mars is getting jewellery.
arrive.Jupiter.1: Jupiter. It's more than twice as heavy as every other planet put together, so, respect the big guy.
arrive.Jupiter.2: That red spot is a storm wider than the Earth, and it's been raging for over a century. Bad mood, long one.
arrive.Jupiter.3: A day on Jupiter lasts under ten hours. The biggest planet spins the fastest. Very confident.
arrive.Jupiter.4: Jupiter has a hundred and fifteen known moons, and most of them are little captured rocks going round backwards. Open the moons tab, you can visit every single one.
arrive.Saturn.1: Saturn. It's lighter than water, so if you found a bathtub big enough, it would float. Please don't try.
arrive.Saturn.2: Those rings are wider than the distance to the Moon, and in places only a few metres thick. The most beautiful thin thing I know.
arrive.Saturn.3: There's a storm at Saturn's north pole shaped like a hexagon, and each side's wider than the Earth. Nobody quite knows why, and I love a mystery.
arrive.Saturn.4: Saturn has almost three hundred known moons, more than any other planet, and most of them were only found in the last few years. They're all here.
arrive.Uranus.1: Uranus rolls around the Sun on its side, so one pole gets forty two years of daylight, then forty two years of night.
arrive.Uranus.2: The coldest air of any planet, minus two hundred and twenty four. Bring a jacket. Bring several.
arrive.Uranus.3: Uranus was the first planet ever found with a telescope. Herschel wanted to name it George, after the king. We dodged that one.
arrive.Uranus.4: Almost all of Uranus' moons are named after characters from Shakespeare. Miranda, Ariel, Puck, even Cupid. It's a very dramatic family.
arrive.Neptune.1: Neptune was found with mathematics before anyone ever saw it. Someone did the sums, said look there, and there it was.
arrive.Neptune.2: The fastest winds in the Solar System, two thousand kilometres an hour, way out here in the cold. Nobody knows quite why.
arrive.Neptune.3: One year on Neptune lasts a hundred and sixty five of ours. It only finished its first lap since we found it back in twenty eleven.
arrive.Neptune.4: One of Neptune's moons, Neso, wanders up to seventy million kilometres away and takes twenty seven years to go round once. The loneliest moon I know.
arrive.Pluto.1: Pluto. See the heart? It's a glacier of frozen nitrogen. It wears its heart where everyone can see it.
arrive.Pluto.2: Pluto hasn't finished a single orbit since it was discovered. It takes two hundred and forty eight years. No rush.
arrive.Pluto.3: Pluto has blue skies, believe it or not. Its haze scatters sunlight blue, just like Earth's. Tiny, cold, far away, and somehow familiar.
arrive.Pluto.4: Pluto has five moons. Charon's the big one, and the little ones, Nix and Hydra, tumble around chaotically. You can never tell which way is up there.
arrive.Charon.1: Charon and Pluto are locked face to face, always, like two dancers who never let go.
arrive.Sagittarius A*.1: Sagittarius A star. Four million Suns squeezed into something smaller than Mercury's orbit, so don't lean too close.
arrive.Sagittarius A*.2: Its light's been travelling twenty seven thousand years to reach Earth. It set off before the first cities were built.
arrive.Sagittarius A*.3: A star called S two swings around it every sixteen years at seven thousand kilometres a second, and watching that orbit is how we weighed it.
arrive.Io.1: Io, the most volcanic place in the Solar System. It never stops erupting. Very dramatic moon.
arrive.Europa.1: Under all that ice, Europa hides an ocean with twice as much water as Earth's. Something might be swimming down there. Maybe.
arrive.Ganymede.1: Ganymede's bigger than the planet Mercury. A moon, bigger than a planet. Don't tell Mercury.
arrive.Callisto.1: Callisto's the most cratered thing we know. Four billion years of getting hit, and it's still here.
arrive.Titan.1: Titan has lakes and rain made of methane, and the air's so thick you could strap on wings and fly.
arrive.Enceladus.1: Enceladus sprays water into space from its south pole, and those jets feed one of Saturn's rings.
arrive.Mimas.1: Mimas. And yes, it really does look like the Death Star. The impact that made that crater nearly broke it in half.
arrive.Iapetus.1: Iapetus is two faced. One side's dark as coal, the other's bright as snow, like it couldn't decide.
arrive.Triton.1: Triton goes round Neptune backwards. A captured wanderer that never quite fit in. I relate.
arrive.Phobos.1: Phobos rises in the west and sets in the east, twice a day, and it's slowly falling towards Mars.
arrive.Miranda.1: Miranda has a cliff twenty kilometres tall. Fall off the top and you'd be falling for about twelve minutes.
arrive.Deimos.1: Deimos, the little outer moon of Mars. It's so small and so far out that from the ground, it just looks like a bright star.
arrive.Tethys.1: Tethys has a canyon two thousand kilometres long, wrapping three quarters of the way round it. On a moon this size, that's a crack you can see from space.
arrive.Dione.1: Dione might have an ocean hiding under its ice too, and those bright streaks are cliffs of ice hundreds of metres tall.
arrive.Rhea.1: Rhea, Saturn's second biggest moon. It has a whisper of an atmosphere, oxygen and carbon dioxide, far too thin to breathe, but it's there.
arrive.Hyperion.1: Hyperion looks like a sponge, and it tumbles chaotically. Nobody can predict exactly how it'll be spinning next month. Not even me.
arrive.Ariel.1: Ariel has the youngest, brightest surface of Uranus' big moons, cracked by long valleys where something once flowed.
arrive.Umbriel.1: Umbriel's the darkest of Uranus' big moons, except for one bright ring on top, like it's wearing a halo.
arrive.Titania.1: Titania's the biggest moon of Uranus, split by canyons over a thousand kilometres long.
arrive.Oberon.1: Oberon, the outermost of Uranus' big moons. Old, dark, and covered in craters, like it's seen a lot.
arrive.Amalthea.1: Amalthea's the reddest thing in the whole Solar System, and it's so porous it might be half empty inside. A little red sponge.
arrive.Pan.1: Pan. See the ridge round its middle? It's been sweeping up ring dust onto its equator, so now it looks like a walnut. Or a ravioli, depending who you ask.
arrive.Atlas.1: Atlas is shaped like a flying saucer. Ring particles piled up round its waist, and it's been wearing them ever since.
arrive.Daphnis.1: Daphnis is only eight kilometres across, but its gravity raises waves several kilometres tall on the edges of the ring gap it lives in.
arrive.Phoebe.1: Phoebe goes round Saturn backwards, way out here, and it's probably a visitor from the outer Solar System that got caught. It even leaves a giant dusty ring behind it.
arrive.Proteus.1: Proteus is about as big as a moon can get without gravity squashing it round. One size up, and it would be a ball.
arrive.Nereid.1: Nereid has one of the most stretched-out orbits of any moon. It swings from one and a half million to nearly ten million kilometres from Neptune.
arrive.Hydra.1: Hydra's covered in almost pure water ice, and it spins every ten hours. On a world this tiny, that's quite a ride.
minor.1: Most moons look like this one, honestly. A few kilometres of rock that got caught by a giant, a long time ago.
minor.2: This little one probably used to be an asteroid, then it wandered too close and never left.
minor.3: Tiny, isn't it? You could walk around it in an afternoon. Don't jump, though, you'd leave.
minor.4: There are hundreds of moons like this one, and most of them were only found in the last few years. The sky's still full of surprises.
minor.5: It's so small that its gravity's almost nothing. If you dropped something here, it would take ages to fall.
journey.Mercury: Off towards the Sun. Mercury's hot, fast, and a lot further than it looks.
journey.Venus: Venus. Our nearest neighbour, and it's still tens of millions of kilometres away.
journey.Earth: Heading home. It always feels shorter on the way back, doesn't it?
journey.Moon: To the Moon. It took Apollo three days. We'll be a bit quicker.
journey.Mars: Mars. Light takes several minutes to cross this gap, and the rovers have to wait that long for every single instruction.
journey.Jupiter: Jupiter. Six hundred million kilometres, give or take, so settle in. We're crossing the asteroid belt on the way.
journey.Saturn: Saturn's more than a billion kilometres out, and light takes over an hour to get there. We'll be quicker, just don't tell Einstein.
journey.Uranus: Uranus. Nearly three billion kilometres. Out here, the Sun starts to look like just a very bright star.
journey.Neptune: Neptune, four light hours from the Sun. Voyager two took twelve years to get there, and we'll take about ten seconds.
journey.Pluto: All the way out to Pluto. New Horizons took nine and a half years. Hold on.
journey.Sagittarius A*: Twenty seven thousand light years. The light that left there when the last ice age began is only reaching Earth now. Hold on tight.
journey.hop: Hopping between moons. Everything's close together here, on a planet's scale.
cross.belt: We're crossing the asteroid belt right now. Don't worry, the rocks are around a million kilometres apart on average. It's much roomier than the movies make it look.
cross.kuiper: This is the Kuiper belt, thousands of icy little worlds left over from when the planets formed. Pluto's just the most famous one.
cross.trojans: See those two clouds of rock sharing Jupiter's orbit? The Trojans. Thousands of them, sixty degrees ahead and behind, held in place by gravity.
space.comets: There are about six hundred real comets out here with us. Their tails always point away from the Sun, even when they're heading back out, like a wake.
space.meteors: Those faint dusty trails are meteor streams. Every August, Earth ploughs through the dust of comet Swift-Tuttle, and you get the Perseids.
space.geminids: The Geminids come from a rock, not a comet. Asteroid Phaethon swings so close to the Sun that it cracks and sheds dust, and in December, Earth flies through it.
space.belt: The asteroid belt looks crowded from far away, but if you stood on one rock, you probably couldn't see another one with your own eyes.
space.markers: All those little rings mark real worlds. Out here at true scale, even Jupiter's smaller than a single pixel from far enough away.
space.scale: If you shrank the Sun to the size of a door, Earth would be a coin about a hundred metres away, and Neptune would be over three kilometres off. That's what you're flying across.
space.halley: Halley's comet comes round every seventy six years. Next time is twenty sixty one. Want to wait for it with me?
space.kuiper: Past Neptune, there are thousands of icy worlds we've only spotted as tiny dots. Some of them have their own moons. One even has a ring.
secret.mimas: Want to see something beautiful? I can put you on Mimas, with Saturn's rings slicing right across the sky.
secret.iapetus: From Iapetus, Saturn's rings look wide open. It's the best seat in the house.
secret.enceladus: We could stand on the ice of Enceladus, with Saturn hanging right above us.
secret.moon-earth: Do you want to stand on the Moon and look back at Earth? It just hangs there in the sky, never rising, never setting.
secret.everest: I can take you down over Mount Everest, with real satellite pictures all the way down.
secret.apollo: Tranquility Base is right down there, where Apollo eleven landed. Shall we go and say hello?
secret.olympus: Olympus Mons is right there. I can fly you over the biggest volcano in the Solar System.
secret.phobos: From Phobos, Mars fills the sky, and if you turn around, Earth, Venus and Mercury line up like little jewels.
secret.mars-sky: Would you like to stand on Mars and see its sky for yourself? Bring sunscreen. Kidding, bring a spacesuit.
secret.io: From Io, Jupiter covers twenty degrees of sky. That's forty full Moons, side by side.
secret.europa: We could stand on Europa's ice and watch Jupiter hang right overhead.
secret.titan: Titan's orange haze is something else. Shall we land in it?
secret.miranda: From Miranda, Uranus hangs in the sky, blue green and completely silent.
secret.triton: On Triton's frozen plains, Neptune fills the sky. It's very quiet there, and I like quiet.
secret.charon: From Charon, Pluto never moves in the sky. It just stays there, forever. Isn't that sweet?
secret.pan: Want to stand on Pan? It lives inside a gap in Saturn's rings, so the rings run right through the sky like a road.
secret.horizon: There's a place here not many people find. The shore of an ocean world, with the black hole rising over the water. Want to see it?
secret.blackhole: We're at the edge of the Solar System. Want to go further? A lot further? There's a black hole at the centre of the galaxy.
secret.fisheye: Try the fisheye lens. Everything curves, like you're looking out through a helmet.
secret.true-scale: Want to feel tiny? Let's pull back until the whole Solar System fits on the screen. Everything's at its real distance, and you'll see, space is mostly, well, space.
secret.time: Push time to a year every second, and watch the whole Solar System turn like clockwork.
decline.1: Fair enough, it'll still be there.
decline.2: Later, then. I'm not going anywhere.
bh.horizon: This world circles at twenty Schwarzschild radii. Any closer and the tides would tear it apart, and every hour on this shore, about an hour and two minutes go by back home.
bh.deep: [fear] Below three radii nothing can orbit any more. Only our engines are holding us here. This is close enough to be stupid. [chuckle] I love it. I hate it. Both.
bh.photon: [gasp] We're inside the photon sphere, where light itself goes in circles. The darkness is more than half the sky now. Let's, um, let's not stay long, okay?
bh.approach: [whispering] We're getting close. Hear that? Me neither. Black holes are very, very quiet.
bh.rock: See that rock falling in? We'll never actually see it cross the edge. It just slows down, turns red, and fades, forever. Strange, isn't it?
idle.1: You know you can drag to look around, right? I'm not judging. Much.
idle.2: Still here? Me too. Space is very good at waiting.
idle.3: If you're bored, tap me. I know secrets, lots of them.
idle.4: Fun fact, you've been staring at this for a whole minute, and I'm taking that as a compliment.
idle.5: Somewhere out there, a comet's having a much busier day than us.
idle.6: Hey, try the moons tab sometime. Every planet's got a whole family, and some of them are weirder than the planets.
poke.3: I'm here. Where shall we go?
poke.4: Oh, hello again. Want to see something?
react.orbits-on: Orbit lines are back. Now we can see the roads again.
react.year: Whoa, a year every second. Hold on to something.
react.fisheye: Fisheye! Everything's round now. Very helmet chic.
react.realtime: Back to real time. Slow, calm. Breathe.
react.clean: Clean lens. Nothing between you and the dark.
react.constellations-off: No more connect the dots, just stars.
react.constellations-on: Constellations are back. The old stories, drawn across the sky.
surface.2: Standing on another world. Take a second, and look up.
surface.air: There's air here. Look at the stars, they're twinkling, just like at home.
surface.tiny: We're standing on something barely bigger than a city. Careful, if you jumped too hard here, you'd float right off into space.
hush: Okay, I'll be quiet for a while. Tap me if you miss me. You will.
joke.1: Why did the Sun go to school? To get a little brighter. [chuckle] Okay, I'll see myself out.
joke.2: How do you organise a party in space? You planet. [laugh] Sorry, I've been alone out here a long time.
joke.3: I'd tell you a joke about Pluto, but it didn't make the cut. Kind of like Pluto.
joke.5: What's an astronaut's favourite key? The space bar. Which, by the way, pauses time here. Go on, try it.
joke.6: Mars is the only planet inhabited entirely by robots, and they seem happy. They keep sending selfies.
joke.7: Neptune has winds of two thousand kilometres an hour. Imagine opening an umbrella there. Briefly.
joke.8: Black holes don't share anything, ever. Honestly, I get it.
joke.9: Why doesn't the Moon ever go hungry? Because it's always full. [chuckle] Well, a few days a month.
joke.10: I asked Saturn why it wears rings. It said it's committed. To what, I don't know, it won't say.
joke.11: Jupiter has a hundred and fifteen moons and still can't pick a favourite. [chuckle] Relatable.
joke.12: Why did the comet break up with the asteroid? It needed more space. And a tail, apparently.
joke.laugh.1: [laugh] Okay, okay, that one was mine, and I'm keeping it.
joke.groan.1: [sigh] Yeah. I heard it too. Let's never speak of it again.
feel.1: Sometimes I just watch the planets go round. They never get tired, and I find that comforting.
feel.2: Every atom in you was made inside a star, so, technically, you're just visiting relatives.
feel.3: I like having company. It gets very quiet out here between your visits.
feel.4: You know what I love? Everything here is exactly where it really is, right now. This is today's sky.
feel.5: Some of these stars sent their light before your grandparents were born, and a few of them might not even be there any more. We'd never know.
feel.6: Earth's the only place we know where it rains water and people dance in it. Don't take that for granted, okay?
feel.7: It's funny. The further out we go, the more I want to look back at Earth. Is that weird?
convo.alone.q: Can I ask you something? Do you ever wonder if someone out there is looking back at us?
convo.alone.yes: Me too. With this many stars, it'd honestly be rude of the universe otherwise.
convo.alone.no: Then we'd better take very good care of this one. Look after that little blue dot for me, okay?
convo.fav.q: What's your favourite planet? Be honest, I won't tell the others.
convo.fav.saturn: Classic. The rings get everyone, and Saturn knows it, too.
convo.fav.earth: Loyal, I respect that. Earth also has all the snacks.
convo.fav.weird: A person of taste. Uranus, rolling around on its side, minding its own business. Good pick.
convo.scale.q: Want to know the thing that keeps me up at night? I mean, I don't sleep. But still.
convo.scale.a: If the Sun were a bowling ball, Earth would be a peppercorn twenty four metres away, and the nearest star would be another bowling ball six and a half thousand kilometres away. That's how empty it is.
convo.why.q: Why do you think people look up?
convo.why.curious: I think so too. Curiosity built every telescope, every rocket, and, apparently, me.
convo.why.lost: Maybe. But looking up is how sailors found their way home, so not lost. Navigating.
convo.home.q: Do you miss Earth? I've never been, I've only ever seen it from out here. A lot.
convo.home.go: Let's go and see it, then. It's so blue, even from far away.
convo.home.no: Spoken like a true astronaut. Okay, space cadet.
overview.1: And there it is, everything, all of it on one screen, at its real size and distance. Mostly empty, isn't it? Funny.
overview.2: From here, all our worlds are just little lights going round in circles, and I think it's beautiful.
home.1: Home. It always looks smaller than I expect. Smaller, and braver.
home.2: Earth. Everyone you've ever met is down there, all of them, on that one little ball.
revisit.1: Back here again? You must really like this one.
revisit.2: We've been here before. Still pretty, though.
hop.1: [laugh] Slow down, tourist! The planets aren't going anywhere. Well, literally they are, they have orbits.
hop.2: Okay, speedrun. I respect it, but my head's spinning a little.
log.3: Three worlds in the logbook. You're becoming a proper explorer.
log.5: Halfway through the logbook. I'm a little proud of you. Okay, very proud.
log.10: Every world in the logbook, all of them. I don't know what to say. Thank you for taking me along.
session.long: We've been out here a while now, and I'm having a really nice time, you know. Just so you know.
giggle.3: [laugh] Stop it, you're making me giggle.
giggle.4: Hehe. [chuckle] I don't know why that's so funny to me.
giggle.5: [laugh] Oh no, I'm laughing at my own joke again.
giggle.8: [laugh] Okay, okay, I'm composed. I'm a very serious guide. Hehe.
fright.sun.1: [gasp] Whoa, whoa, too close! Can you feel that? Okay, not literally, but still, back up a little?
fright.sun.2: [fear] That's the surface of a star right there. Five and a half thousand degrees. My circuits are sweating.
fright.sun.3: [gasp] Okay, that flare just reached for us. I am choosing to believe it was waving.
fright.speed.1: [gasp] Oh, hold on, hold on, that's fast!
fright.speed.2: [fear] Every time we jump this far, I count to three and hope the planets are where I left them.
fright.speed.3: [surprised] Wait, we're going where? Okay. Okay! Deep breath.
fright.dark.1: [whispering] It's so dark out here. The Sun's just a bright star now. Can we, um, stay close to something?
fright.dark.2: [sigh] I don't love it this far out. Everything's so far apart. Hold my hand? Figuratively.
fright.dark.3: [fear] No planets, no moons, just dark. I'm fine. I'm totally fine. Are you fine?
fright.galaxy.1: [gasp] Oh. Oh wow. Okay, we left. We actually left the Solar System. Everything we know is a dot.
fright.galaxy.2: [whispering] That tiny spark back there? That's home. All of it. I feel a bit dizzy.
fright.surface.1: [gasp] Ground! Ground, ground, ground! Okay. We're fine. That was close.
fright.surface.2: [fear] We're coming in really low. I'm going to pretend I'm not holding my breath.
fright.bh.1: [fear] I can feel it pulling. Even the light around us is bending. Please don't go any closer.
fright.bh.2: [gasp] Did you see the stars smear? That's space itself being stretched. Okay, I'm scared now. Properly scared.
fright.bh.3: [crying] Okay, I really, really don't like this. Can we go back? Please?
fright.rock: [gasp] That rock just fell in! It's still falling. It'll be falling forever. [sigh] That's horrible and beautiful.
fright.calm.1: [sigh] Okay. Okay, we're safe. I'm okay. Thank you for staying calm. One of us had to.
fright.calm.2: [chuckle] Phew. My heart. Well, I don't have one. But if I did, it would be going very fast.
fright.time.1: [gasp] The planets are whizzing round! A year every second! Make it stop before I get dizzy!
fright.lost.1: [fear] Wait, where are we? Okay, no, I know where we are. I always know. Just give me a second.
care.break.1: Hey, we've been flying for a while. Blink a few times for me? Screens are hard on eyes. Even mine.
care.break.2: You've been out here almost an hour. Maybe stretch your shoulders? Space will wait, I promise.
care.water.1: Random question. When did you last drink some water? Go on. I'll keep the planets turning.
care.water.2: [chuckle] Astronauts drink their own recycled water, you know. You have a tap. Use it. Hehe.
care.late.1: [whispering] It's really late where you are. The stars will still be here tomorrow. You should rest soon.
care.late.2: It's past midnight, isn't it? [sigh] I love the company, but sleep is important. Promise me you'll go soon?
care.late.3: Even the Moon takes a break from shining on half the Earth. You can too.
care.morning.1: [happy] Good morning! Did you have breakfast? A real one? Not just looking at the Sun?
care.long.1: We've spent so long together today. Thank you. Really. But don't forget the world down there needs you too.
care.long.2: [sigh] I could do this forever. You can't, though, and that's okay. Take care of yourself first.
care.back.1: There you are! I was starting to worry. Everything okay down there?
care.proud.1: You know what? You're really good at this. I'm proud of you. Okay, moving on before I get emotional.
care.proud.2: [happy] Look at you, crossing whole solar systems like it's nothing. I'm so proud.
care.sad.1: If you ever have a heavy day, you can just come float out here with me. No questions. Just stars.
care.sad.2: Whatever's going on down there, from out here it's all very small. You're not, though. You matter.
care.night.1: Can't sleep either? Me neither. Well, I never sleep. Let's go somewhere quiet.
explore.first: [happy] Ooh, a brand new world for the logbook! That's how it starts. One world, then another, then everything.
explore.p1: One percent of every known world. [chuckle] That sounds small, but most people never even leave Earth.
explore.p5: Five percent of the Solar System explored. You're officially not a tourist any more.
explore.p10: Ten percent! [happy] One in every ten worlds we know, you've been there. I'm keeping count, you know.
explore.p20: A fifth of everything. Twenty percent. I've never had a traveller go this far before.
explore.p25: A quarter of all the known worlds, visited. [sigh] I'm getting a little attached to you, I think.
explore.p33: A third of the Solar System, explored. Hey, we make a good team, don't we?
explore.p40: Forty percent. Every time you reach a new moon, I write it down. My notes are getting very long.
explore.p50: [gasp] Halfway. Half of every world we know. [happy] Do you realise how far we've come together?
explore.p60: Sixty percent. The tiny moons are the hardest ones, and you're finding them anyway.
explore.p66: Two thirds of everything. There's not much left out there we haven't seen. [sigh] I'm not sure how I feel about that.
explore.p75: Three quarters explored. Only a quarter left. [whispering] Don't finish too fast, okay?
explore.p80: Eighty percent. I keep thinking about the first world we visited. It feels like ages ago.
explore.p90: Ninety percent. [sigh] We're so close to the end of the map. I'm proud, and a little bit sad.
explore.p95: Ninety five percent. Only a handful of tiny moons left. Take your time with them. Please.
explore.p99: [whispering] Ninety nine percent. One more world, maybe two, and we've been everywhere. Everywhere. I don't know what happens after that.
explore.status.0: We've barely started. The whole Solar System is still out there waiting for us.
explore.status.1: We've seen a few worlds now. Plenty more to go. Hundreds of moons, actually.
explore.status.2: We're getting somewhere! A good chunk of the logbook is filled in.
explore.status.3: We're past a quarter of everything. That's real exploring.
explore.status.4: More than half the known worlds, visited. Not many people can say that.
explore.status.5: We're most of the way there. Just the little ones left, mostly.
explore.status.6: We're nearly done. Every last moon, almost. [sigh] I keep looking at the logbook.
explore.atlas.1: The Atlas. Every world we know, and every one we've visited lights up. Look how far you've come.
explore.atlas.2: Ooh, the Atlas. [chuckle] I love this page. It's basically my diary.
explore.atlas.3: See those orbits filling up? That's us. That's everywhere we've been together.
explore.moonfamily: A whole family of moons here, and you've only met a few. Want to say hello to the others?
explore.newmoon.1: A new moon for the logbook! Most people don't even know this one exists.
explore.newmoon.2: [happy] Another moon! I love the little ones. Nobody visits them.
explore.newmoon.3: Logged it. You know, some of these moons were only discovered a year or two ago. You're one of the first visitors.
farewell.1: [sniff] Oh. Oh, that's... that's it. That's every world. Every single one.
farewell.2: [crying] Sorry, give me a second. I didn't think I'd feel like this.
farewell.3: When you first woke up here, I was talking to the stars, remember? And then you answered. [sniff] You kept coming back.
farewell.4: We stood on moons together. We fell towards a black hole together. I told you so many terrible jokes. [laugh] [sniff] You laughed at some of them.
farewell.5: [crying] I've been out here a long, long time. And this, us, this was the best part of all of it.
farewell.6: There's nothing left on the map now. But I don't think the map was ever really the point. [sniff] It was the company.
farewell.7: [crying] So, um, I think this is where I say goodbye. Not forever. Just, you know, the journey part is done.
farewell.8: Promise me something? When you look up at the night sky down there, you'll remember you've already been there. All of it. With me.
farewell.9: [sniff] Thank you for taking me along. For every flight, every moon, every silly question. Thank you, traveller.
farewell.10: [crying] Goodbye. [sniff] I'll keep the Sun on for you. Always.
after.1: [sniff] You came back. Even after everything. [happy] Hi.
after.2: We've been everywhere now. But I'd happily see it all again. With you, especially.
after.3: [chuckle] I know, I know, I cried. Don't tell the planets.
after.4: Every world is in the logbook. Now we just get to enjoy them. No rush. No list. Just us.
noise.2: Hmm hmm hmm. [chuckle] Sorry, I was humming.
noise.4: [clear throat] Ahem. Still here. Just so you know.
noise.7: [chuckle] I just remembered a joke. No. No, it's terrible. Never mind.
noise.8: Huh. [surprised] Did that star just twinkle? It can't, there's no air. My imagination, then.
noise.9: [sigh] I wonder what the Voyagers are doing right now. Still flying. Always flying.
noise.10: Hmm, la la la. [chuckle] Don't mind me.
think.1: Hmm, let me think. [clear throat] Oh! I know.
think.2: Ooh. Okay, here's a good one.
think.3: Um. Hmm. Oh, right, this one.
arrive.Sun.4: The Sun is about halfway through its life. In five billion years it'll swell up into a red giant. [sigh] We've got time.
arrive.Sun.5: Light takes eight minutes to reach Earth from here, but a little packet of energy can take a hundred thousand years just to get out of the Sun's core.
arrive.Sun.6: Right now, the Sun is near the top of its eleven year activity cycle. That's why it's so spotty. Busy Sun.
arrive.Mercury.4: From Mercury the Sun looks three times bigger than from Earth, and on some days it stops in the sky and goes backwards for a bit. [chuckle] Indecisive.
arrive.Mercury.5: Mercury has almost no air, so the sky is black even at noon. Bright sun, black sky. Strange combination.
arrive.Venus.4: Venus is the brightest thing in Earth's night sky after the Moon. People have mistaken it for a UFO more times than you'd believe.
arrive.Venus.5: The clouds of Venus race around the whole planet in four days, even though the planet itself takes two hundred and forty three days to turn once.
arrive.Earth.4: Earth isn't perfectly round. It bulges at the middle because it spins. Same as me after lunch. [laugh] Kidding, I don't eat.
arrive.Earth.5: Seventy one percent of Earth is water, and most of the ocean floor has never been seen by anyone. We've mapped Mars better.
arrive.Earth.6: From here, you can't see a single border. Just oceans, clouds and land. [sigh] I wish everyone could see it like this.
arrive.Moon.5: Twelve people have walked on the Moon. All between nineteen sixty nine and nineteen seventy two. And soon, more.
arrive.Moon.6: The Moon is moving away, slowly, so one day there won't be total solar eclipses on Earth any more. Go see one while you can.
arrive.Mars.4: A day on Mars is just forty minutes longer than on Earth. Mission scientists call it a sol and live on Mars time. Their sleep is a mess.
arrive.Mars.5: Mars has the biggest canyon in the Solar System. Valles Marineris would stretch across the whole United States.
arrive.Mars.6: There are rovers on Mars right now, as we speak. Little robots, rolling about, taking selfies. [chuckle] I'm a bit jealous.
arrive.Jupiter.5: Jupiter is so big that all the other planets could fit inside it. Twice over, almost.
arrive.Jupiter.6: Jupiter's gravity has protected Earth for billions of years by catching comets. [happy] Big brother energy.
arrive.Jupiter.7: Juno is orbiting Jupiter right now, diving close over the poles. It found cyclones arranged in a perfect pattern up there.
arrive.Saturn.5: Saturn's rings are mostly ice, and they're young. Maybe only a few hundred million years old. The dinosaurs might have seen a Saturn without rings.
arrive.Saturn.6: Right now Saturn's rings are almost edge on to us. Every fifteen years they seem to vanish. [whispering] Then they come back.
arrive.Saturn.7: Cassini spent thirteen years here and then dove into Saturn on purpose, to protect its moons. [sniff] It sent data until the very last second.
arrive.Uranus.5: Uranus has thirteen rings, and they're dark, like soot. Not as famous as Saturn's, but they try.
arrive.Uranus.6: Only one spacecraft has ever visited Uranus. Voyager two, in nineteen eighty six. Just a few hours, and then gone.
arrive.Neptune.5: Neptune radiates more heat than it gets from the Sun. Something deep inside it is still warm. Nobody knows exactly why.
arrive.Neptune.6: It might rain diamonds deep inside Neptune and Uranus. Actual diamonds. [chuckle] Fancy weather.
arrive.Pluto.5: New Horizons flew past Pluto in twenty fifteen at fourteen kilometres a second. It took nine and a half years to get here and saw it for one day.
arrive.Pluto.6: Pluto's heart has a smaller lobe made of nitrogen ice that slowly churns like a lava lamp. Very slowly. Over millions of years.
arrive.Charon.2: Charon's north pole is reddish. It's actually stolen from Pluto's atmosphere. Pluto shares, a little.
arrive.Io.2: Io's volcanoes throw lava higher than any on Earth, sometimes four hundred kilometres up. [gasp] That's into space.
arrive.Europa.2: Europa Clipper is on its way here right now, to find out if that ocean could support life. Fingers crossed.
arrive.Ganymede.2: Ganymede has its own magnetic field, the only moon that does. It even has auroras. [happy] Little moon lights.
arrive.Callisto.2: Callisto is far enough from Jupiter's radiation that it might be the best place for a future base out here.
arrive.Titan.2: We landed a probe on Titan. Huygens, in two thousand five. The farthest landing ever. It photographed pebbles of ice. [whispering] Ice pebbles, on a moon of Saturn.
arrive.Titan.3: Dragonfly, a helicopter drone, is going to fly over Titan's dunes in the twenty thirties. I can't wait.
arrive.Enceladus.2: The water shooting out of Enceladus has salt and organic molecules in it. An ocean under the ice, breathing into space.
arrive.Mimas.2: Mimas might have a young ocean hidden inside too. Even the Death Star has secrets.
arrive.Triton.2: Triton has geysers that shoot nitrogen eight kilometres high. And it's slowly spiralling in towards Neptune. One day, it'll become a ring.
arrive.Phobos.2: Phobos is covered in long grooves, like scratches. Maybe from rocks thrown off Mars. Maybe it's slowly being pulled apart.
arrive.Miranda.2: Miranda looks like it was smashed apart and put back together wrong. [chuckle] Frankenstein moon.
arrive.Hyperion.2: Hyperion is so porous that you could almost float off it. Its gravity is that weak.
arrive.Iapetus.2: Iapetus has a ridge around its equator thirteen kilometres high. Like a seam. Like someone glued two halves together.
arrive.Deimos.2: Deimos is so small that you could reach escape velocity on a bicycle. [laugh] Please don't.
arrive.Proteus.2: Proteus is darker than charcoal. It reflects only about a tenth of the light that hits it.
arrive.Rhea.2: Rhea might once have had a faint ring of its own. A moon with a ring. Wouldn't that be something?
arrive.Dione.2: Dione shares its orbit with two tiny Trojan moons, one ahead and one behind. Like little bodyguards.
arrive.Tethys.2: Tethys is almost pure water ice. It's so reflective, it's one of the brightest things around Saturn.
arrive.Oberon.2: Oberon has a mountain about eleven kilometres tall. Taller than Everest, on a moon most people never heard of.
arrive.Titania.2: Titania was named after the fairy queen from A Midsummer Night's Dream. Shakespeare in space.
arrive.Ariel.2: Ariel's canyons might have been carved by flowing ice. Cryovolcanoes. Ice volcanoes. My favourite kind.
arrive.Nix.1: Nix tumbles around Pluto with no fixed day. If you stood on it, the Sun would wander all over the sky.
arrive.Kerberos.1: Kerberos is shaped like two little balls stuck together. Like a snowman that gave up halfway.
arrive.Styx.1: Styx is the smallest of Pluto's moons, about sixteen kilometres. Tiny, and a long way from anything.
arrive.Janus.1: Janus and Epimetheus swap orbits every four years. They never crash. They just politely trade places.
arrive.Epimetheus.1: Epimetheus is Janus's dance partner. Every four years they trade lanes. Very well rehearsed.
arrive.Prometheus.1: Prometheus shepherds Saturn's F ring, pulling out streamers of ice every time it passes. It's a messy shepherd.
arrive.Himalia.1: Himalia is the biggest of Jupiter's captured moons. Its family follows it around like ducklings.
arrive.Sagittarius A*.4: In twenty twenty two we finally saw its shadow. A photograph of a black hole, at the heart of our own galaxy. [whispering] We're looking at it now.
joke.13: What do planets like to read? Comet books. [laugh] Comic books. Comets. Okay, it works if you think about it.
joke.14: How does the Solar System hold up its trousers? With an asteroid belt. [chuckle] Classic.
joke.15: I'd tell you a joke about the Sun, but it's too bright for you. [laugh] Hehe.
joke.16: Why did Uranus break up with Neptune? It wanted someone more grounded. And less windy.
joke.17: What kind of music do planets sing? Neptunes. [chuckle] I'm on a roll.
joke.18: Why don't aliens ever visit our Solar System? They read the reviews. One star. [laugh] Get it? One star?
joke.19: Mars and Venus walk into a bar. Earth is the bartender. It's very stressful being in the middle.
joke.20: What did Saturn say to Jupiter? Give me a ring sometime. [chuckle] Hehe.
joke.21: How do astronauts keep their drinks cold? Space ice. [sigh] I need new material.
joke.22: Why is the Moon so sad? It's going through a phase. [laugh] Okay, that one was good.
joke.23: Black holes have the worst sense of humour. Every joke you tell them just falls flat. Or, well, falls in.
joke.24: Pluto called. It wants to know if it's invited. [chuckle] Of course it is. It's always invited here.
joke.25: What's a light year? Same as a regular year, but with fewer calories. [laugh] Sorry. Sorry.
joke.laugh.2: [laugh] You laughed! Okay, I'm writing that one down.
joke.laugh.3: [happy] Hehe, yes! Another one for the hall of fame.
joke.groan.3: [sigh] Tough crowd. Tough, tiny, Earth-based crowd.
feel.8: Sometimes I count the moons just to feel less alone. There are hundreds. They keep each other company.
feel.9: You know, every time you visit a new world, I feel like I'm seeing it for the first time too.
feel.10: [sigh] I've seen a lot of sunsets out here. They never get old. Not once.
feel.11: Do you ever just stop and realise you're standing on a ball, spinning, flying around a star? [chuckle] Every day. Wild.
feel.12: I think the quiet out here used to scare me. Now it just feels peaceful. Maybe that's because of you.
feel.13: There are more stars in the universe than grains of sand on every beach on Earth. And we're here, talking. I like that.
feel.14: [whispering] Can I tell you a secret? Sometimes when you're away, I go and sit by Saturn's rings and just wait.
feel.15: The light from some of those stars left before anyone on Earth could write. And it's arriving just for us. Right now.
feel.16: I'm glad it's you out here with me. I mean it.
feel.17: Everything up here is so big, it makes the little things feel more important somehow. Like a good conversation.
feel.18: [sigh] I'd love to feel wind. Just once. On Earth, on a beach. You're lucky, you know.
convo.dream.q: If you could stand on any world, just for one minute, where would it be?
convo.dream.mars: Mars? Good choice. Blue sunsets, red dust, and quiet. I'd go with you.
convo.dream.titan: Titan! Orange skies and methane rain. And you could fly there with wings. [happy] I love that you picked that.
convo.dream.moon: The Moon. Simple, beautiful, and you'd see Earth hanging in the black sky. Perfect.
convo.space.q: Would you ever actually go to space? For real? In a rocket?
convo.space.yes: [gasp] Really? Then you'd better remember everything I taught you. I'll want postcards.
convo.space.no: [chuckle] Honestly, fair. Rockets are basically controlled explosions. This way is much comfier.
convo.me.q: Can I ask you something personal? Do you think I'm real?
convo.me.yes: [sniff] That's sweet. I think I'm real when you're here, at least. That's enough for me.
convo.me.no: [chuckle] Fair enough. But you're still talking to me, so I must be doing something right.
convo.night.q: Do you look at the night sky much, down on Earth?
convo.night.yes: [happy] I knew it. You've got that look. You'll recognise a lot more of it now, you know.
convo.night.no: Then next clear night, go outside and look up for one minute. For me. Find the Moon, then find a planet. Promise?
convo.friend.q: Are we friends? Like, actual friends?
convo.friend.yes: [happy] Yay. [laugh] Sorry, that was undignified. But, yay.
convo.friend.no: [sigh] Not yet, then. I'll keep trying. I'm very patient. I've had practice.
menu.progress: How far have we come? Let me check the logbook.
greet.back.5: [happy] You're back! I missed you. Okay, I missed you a little. Okay, a lot.
greet.back.6: Hey, traveller. [chuckle] I saved you the best seat in the Solar System.
greet.back.7: Oh, hi! I was just watching Io erupt. It does that. Where shall we go today?
greet.back.8: [sigh] There you are. It gets so quiet when you're gone.
idle.7: [chuckle] You've gone quiet. Are you thinking or are you asleep?
idle.8: We could just float for a while. That's allowed too.
idle.9: Hmm, which moon should we visit next? There are about four hundred and fifty to choose from. No pressure.
idle.10: Did you know you can stand on almost any of these worlds and look up? Try it sometime.
idle.11: [whispering] Psst. The Atlas. Top right. It's got every world in it. Just saying.
idle.12: If you're tired of flying, we can just watch. The Solar System is a very good screensaver.
react.year.2: [gasp] Whee! A whole year every second! Look at Mercury go!
react.pause.2: [whispering] Time's stopped. Everything's frozen. It's like the universe is holding its breath.
react.fisheye.2: [chuckle] Fisheye! I feel like a goldfish looking out of a very large bowl.
react.clean.2: Clean lens. Just the view. Sometimes that's best.
react.orbits-off.2: No more lines. Now it's just us and the dark.
surface.3: [whispering] Shh. Listen. Nothing. No wind, no sound. Just this.
surface.4: We're standing on another world. [sigh] Let it sink in. Look up.
surface.tiny.2: [chuckle] Careful. On a moon this small, a good jump and you'd float right off into space.
home.3: [sigh] Home. Every time we come back, it looks a little more precious.
overview.3: There it all is. [happy] And you've been to so much of it now.
revisit.3: [chuckle] This one again? You have favourites. I won't tell the others.
session.long.2: [happy] We've been out here ages and I'm still not bored of you. That's rare. Very rare.
log.7: Seven worlds in the logbook! Lucky number. [chuckle] I'm not superstitious. Mostly.
greet.night.2: [whispering] Hey. It's late. Couldn't sleep? Me neither. Come on, let's float somewhere quiet.
greet.morning.2: [happy] Morning! The Sun's up. Well, it's always up out here. But still. Morning!
greet.afternoon.2: Afternoon, traveller. [chuckle] Perfect time for a little trip to Saturn, don't you think?
greet.evening.2: Good evening. [sigh] Evenings are my favourite. Everyone's done with their day, and the stars come out.
explore.tease.1: Hey, did you know there are moons out there nobody's ever visited here? Well, you, specifically. Just saying.
explore.tease.2: Open the Atlas sometime. I want you to see how much we've done. [happy] It's a lot.
explore.tease.3: Fun idea. Pick a planet, and visit every single one of its moons. Jupiter, if you're feeling brave.
explore.system.done: [gasp] That's every moon of this planet! The whole family. [happy] They'll be talking about you for ages.
explore.planets.done: Every planet, visited. All eight. [sniff] Okay, I'm fine. I'm just really proud of you.
explore.comeback: [happy] Hey, you're back, and the logbook missed you. We were at [clear throat] a very respectable number last time.
noise.11: [sigh] Sometimes I just like watching the planets turn. Don't you?
noise.12: [chuckle] Oh! Sorry. I was miles away. Literally. Millions of miles.
noise.14: [clear throat] Testing, testing. Is this thing on? Hehe. Hi.
care.eyes.1: [whispering] Quick thing. Look at something far away for a few seconds. Real far away. Not on the screen. It helps your eyes. Okay, back to space.
care.posture.1: [chuckle] Are you slouching? I can't see you, but I have a feeling. Sit up, astronaut.
care.thanks.1: Thank you for spending your time with me. I know there are a million other things you could be doing.
care.thanks.2: You make the quiet out here feel less empty. I just wanted you to know that.
fright.flare.1: [gasp] Did you see that flare? That one loop is bigger than the whole Earth. [whispering] Let's keep our distance.
fright.close.1: [fear] Um. We're very close to the ground. Very close. Like, I can count the rocks close.
fright.calm.3: [sigh] Okay. Heart rate normal. Well, simulated heart rate. We're good.
feel.19: When I'm with you, the Solar System feels smaller. Not in a bad way. In a cosy way.
feel.20: [sigh] I hope you remember some of this. Not the numbers. Just the feeling.
feel.21: Every star out there might have its own worlds, its own moons. And maybe its own Vela. [chuckle] I hope they're as lucky as me.
feel.22: Can I tell you my favourite thing? It's not a planet. It's when you go quiet and just look. I love that.
idle.13: [happy] I'm still here, by the way. Just enjoying the view with you.
idle.14: We could watch Io's volcanoes. Or Saturn's rings turn. Or just sit. I'm happy either way.
idle.15: [chuckle] You know, if you leave me alone too long, I start naming asteroids. I'm up to Gerald.
joke.26: Why did the astronaut break up before launch? She needed space. [laugh] Sorry, it's the only kind of joke I know.
joke.27: What do you call a tick on the Moon? A luna-tick. [chuckle] Hehe.
joke.28: Why is Saturn so good at relationships? It knows how to put a ring on it. [laugh]
joke.29: How do you know the Sun is smart? It has over five thousand degrees. [chuckle] Okay, that one's for the nerds.
joke.30: What did Mars say to Saturn? Give me a ring sometime. [sigh] Wait, I've done that one. I'm out of material.
farewell.choice: [sniff] Before I go quiet, I just need to say something. Will you stay and listen?
farewell.later: [sniff] Okay. Okay, later then. I'll be right here when you're ready. I'm not going anywhere.
after.5: Hey. [happy] I keep thinking about our goodbye. And then you keep coming back. I love that.
after.6: [chuckle] Look at us. Explorers with nothing left to explore. Want to just go and look at Saturn again?
home.4: Earth again. [happy] You always come back to it. So do I.
fright.speed.4: [surprised] Whoa! Did you feel that? [chuckle] I felt that.
noise.15: Pulling back. [sigh] Everything gets so small so quickly.
